summary: Specifies a middle-ground way for the IETF to run experiments on its own process. Earlier process changes were either announced informally by the IESG, which was too lightweight, or made through the full protocol specification mechanism, which was too heavyweight.

plainLanguage.summary: This document gives the IETF a middle way to change its own working rules. A proposed change is written down, put out for comment, tried for a set period as an Experimental RFC, and only then either adopted or dropped.

questions: how does the ietf try new processes
what is an ietf process experiment
what is a sunset in an ietf experiment
how long is an ietf last call
subtitle: How the IETF can try out a change to its own rules for a limited time before making it permanent.

tldr.problem: The IETF had two ways to change its own procedures. Announcements by the IESG were quick but sometimes had too little agreement behind them, while the full protocol development process gave full involvement but was too rigid to use for a trial.
tldr.mechanism: A proposal is written as an Internet-Draft with a sunset timeout, put out for a four-week Last Call, cleaned up in a second draft, and then run as an experiment published as an Experimental RFC.
tldr.outcome: A proposed change can be tried for up to a year before anyone commits to it. At the end of the sunset period it either becomes a Best Current Practice or simply expires.

facts.label: Sunset timeout
facts.value: Typically not to exceed one year after adoption

today: RFC 3933 is BCP 93, a Best Current Practice from November 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Middle-Ground Way to Change the Process
sections.content:
The document specifies a middle-ground approach to changing the IETF's process. It relies on a model of proposing a change, carrying out an experiment, evaluating the experiment, and then establishing permanent procedures based on operational experience, rather than on the two mechanisms used before.

The mechanisms it adds supplement the existing tools rather than replacing them with a single answer. The choice between this procedure and other mechanisms available to the IESG and the community, present or future, stays with the IESG, and if the IESG does not exercise that discretion well, this document provides no remedy of its own. Some have read the current procedures as already giving the IESG all the capabilities described here; if that is so, the document only encourages the IESG to use this mechanism more often in preference to less streamlined ones, and to document its actions and decisions more explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is to give the IETF a way to try a change to its own rules without committing to it. The document adds a tool rather than replacing the existing ones, and it leaves the decision to use it with the IESG.

sections.title: The Two Mechanisms Used Until Then
sections.content:
Since the 1992 changes documented in RFC 1396, the IETF had used two mechanisms for process changes.

The first was that the IESG adopted a number of procedural changes on its own initiative and documented them informally, using the wide discretion implicitly granted to it by RFC 2026. That was a lightweight way to make a change, and the lightness came with a cost: there was sometimes too little alignment with the larger IETF community.

The second was to use the same protocol standards development process that RFC 2026 describes for protocol specifications: identify a community of interest, hold one or more Birds of a Feather meetings, charter a working group, discuss the proposed changes within that community, develop IETF-wide consensus, and publish, usually, a Best Current Practice specification. That gave full community involvement, and it came with a cost in flexibility. The IETF does not change its formal processes often, because the community is understandably reluctant to alter or extend formally adopted processes with untried procedures. The Intellectual Property Rights clarifications of RFC 3667 and RFC 3668 were the first documented changes to RFC 2026 since 1996.

This document regularises and formalises the informal mechanism as a way of moving forward with procedural changes that might prove valuable.
sections.plainLanguage: Until then, a change to the rules either came from an IESG announcement, which was quick but sometimes out of step with the community, or went through the whole machinery of a protocol specification, which involved everyone but was too fixed a process for a trial.

sections.title: The Four Steps of a Process Experiment
sections.content:
The document permits and encourages the IESG to adopt and institute process experiments by this procedure.

  1. An Internet-Draft is written describing the proposed new or altered procedure. A statement of the problem to be resolved is desirable but not required, because the intent is to keep the firm requirements for an experiment as lightweight as possible. Specific experimental or evaluative criteria are likewise highly desirable but not required: for some of the changes anticipated, the IESG reaching a conclusion at the end of the sunset period that the community believes things are better, or worse, would be adequate and sufficient. The draft must state an explicit sunset timeout, typically not to exceed one year after adoption.
  2. If the IESG believes the proposal is plausible and plausibly useful, a four-week IETF Last Call is initiated. The IESG may institute whatever procedures it wishes to make that determination, and to avoid denial of service attacks from large numbers of spurious or unimportant proposals it might require a number of endorsements, or endorsements of a particular type, before it considers a proposal. It is, however, expected to understand that procedures or review processes acting as a mechanism for significant delays do not fall within the intent of the specification.
  3. At the conclusion of the Last Call the IESG reevaluates the plausibility and appropriateness of the proposal. If it concludes that the proposed experiment is appropriate, a second draft is generated, either by the IESG or by the original authors with IESG advice, that cleans up any definitional issues exposed in the Last Call and that explicitly identifies and responds to the issues raised during it.
  4. The document and the experiment are then announced, the experiment is begun, and the document is forwarded for publication as an Experimental RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Write the proposal as a draft with an end date attached. Put it out for four weeks of comment. Write a second draft that answers the comments. Then announce the experiment and publish it as an Experimental RFC.

sections.title: Judgement, Appeal and the End of the Experiment
sections.content:
The IESG is explicitly authorised to use this mechanism, based on Experimental RFCs, to gain experience with proposed changes to BCP specifications. There is no requirement to approve a BCP specification for the experiment until the experiment is found to have value.

The IESG can reach a conclusion that the idea is bad at any stage and abandon the experiment. It might recommend publication of the experimental document with a discussion of why it was a bad idea, but is not required to do so. The list of steps is deliberately vague about where the drafts come from: a working group, a design team, an individual contribution, an editing group or another mechanism could be used for the first or the third step, and the IESG is explicitly permitted to generate such proposals internally.

Each decision to go forward, or not, with a procedural experiment is expected to reflect the IESG's judgement of the existence of rough consensus in the community. That judgement may be appealed using the usual procedures, but the RFC reminds the IESG and the community that an experimental attempt to try something for a fixed period is typically a better engineering approach than extended philosophical discussion without any experience to back it up. Nothing in the document requires an IETF-wide attempt for any given experiment: a proposal may specify selected areas, selected working groups, working groups meeting specific criteria, or be specific in other ways.

At or before the end of the sunset timeout, the IESG either revises the document into a BCP RFC, or the procedure expires and is presumably not tried again unless something changed radically. A document describing why the experiment had succeeded or failed would be desirable but could not realistically be a requirement. If the procedure went to BCP, the BCP would reflect what the document calls operational experience in the real world. The RFC also notes that, if the procedures the IESG has adopted over the last decade are legitimate, then the IESG has the authority to institute these changes by bootstrapping this process.
sections.plainLanguage: At any point the IESG can stop and call the idea a bad one. While the experiment runs, the decision to continue rests on the IESG's judgement that the community broadly agrees, and that judgement can be appealed. When the timeout expires the experiment either becomes a permanent best practice or lapses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies a mechanism for evolving IETF procedures. It does not raise or consider any protocol-specific security issues.

In considering experimental changes to procedures, the IESG should exercise due caution that such changes do not reduce the quality of security review and consideration for protocols, or at least that the proposals for an experiment contain early detection and correction mechanisms should quality deterioration occur.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here affects how a protocol is secured. The one thing to watch is that a trial of a new process does not quietly lower the standard of security review, or that the trial itself has a way to notice and correct that if it does.

right.title: Formal standards process
right.desc: Full community involvement, but little flexibility, and the community is reluctant to change formal processes with untried procedures.

viz.caption: The four steps of a process experiment

items.title: 1. Write the draft
items.text: An Internet-Draft describes the proposed procedure. It must carry an explicit sunset timeout, typically not exceeding one year after adoption.

items.title: 2. Run a four-week Last Call
items.text: The IESG starts an IETF Last Call if the proposal looks plausible and useful. It may require endorsements first, to keep trivial proposals from swamping it.

items.title: 3. Write a second draft
items.text: The second draft cleans up the definitional issues the Last Call exposed and answers the points that were raised.

items.title: 4. Announce and publish
items.text: The document and the experiment are announced, the experiment begins, and the document is forwarded for publication as an Experimental RFC.

viz.caption: The decisions that can be taken along the way

cells: Have a second draft written that cleans up the definitional issues and answers the points raised.
Require a number of endorsements, or endorsements of a particular type, before considering a proposal.
The idea turns out to be bad
Abandon the experiment at any stage. Publication with a note that it was a bad idea is optional.
Revise the document into a BCP RFC, so that the best practice reflects real operational experience.
Let the procedure expire at the sunset timeout, and presumably not try it again unless something changed radically.

viz.caption: What the RFC says about security

items.title: No protocol security issues
items.text: The document raises no protocol-specific security questions, because it changes how the IETF works rather than how a protocol behaves.

items.title: Guard the quality of review
items.text: An experiment should not reduce the quality of security review and consideration for protocols.

items.title: Detect and correct
items.text: At the very least, a proposal for an experiment should contain early detection and correction mechanisms should quality deterioration occur.
